To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the catchment area of the Filchner-Ronnen Ice Shelf, East Antarctica, has been thickening since 1992, and that the thickening is consistent with a combination of 20th Century precipitation increases and continuing response to a Holocene precipitation increase. [2]
the Filchner-Ronné catchment area thickened by 39 ± 25 Gton/yr from 1992 to 2007, and that this thickening is consistent with altimeter measurements of elevation change.

the Filchner-Ronné catchment has thinned since the early Holocene by ∼0.2 m/yr, and has thickened in the 20th Century by ∼1.2 m/ yr. [2] The ice sheet that covers East Antarctica has a volume of ∼30 million cubic km, which is more than 10 times the volume of the Greenland Ice Sheet.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ice-sheet mass balance in the region of the Filchner-Ronné ice shelf.
the ice sheet mass budget and the processes that determine its change.
the mass balance of the Filchner-Ronn Ice Shelf catchment, which is one of the largest catchment areas of the Antarctic ice sheet.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the East Antarctic Ice Sheet is currently accumulating, with a net gain of ice mass.
the ice sheet has been thickening, and that this thickening is likely to continue for the foreseeable future. [2]
the mass-balance estimates of the Filchner-Ronn ice shelf catchment area are in better agreement than previously thought. [2]
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Filchner-Ronnen catchment has been thickening at an increasing rate since the mid-20th Century. [1]
the Filchner-Ronni Ice Shelf is currently in balance, but that it has thinned by ∼0.5 meters per year over the last century. [2]
the ice streams in the catchment area of the Filchner-Ronn Ice Shelf are thickening, and that the ice sheet is in balance. [2]
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ice streams that drain the East Antarctic ice sheet are currently gaining mass, and that this mass gain is likely to be sustained into the foreseeable future.

the East Antarctic plateau is not in steady state and that it may have been accumulating ice for at least the last several thousand years, which is consistent with the recent finding of a large accumulation anomaly in the West Antarctic ice sheet.
the Filchner-Ronnes catchment is thickening at a rate that is consistent with the altimeter observations.
